prompt: According to MOD-2.I.1, in the long run and in the absence of government policy actions, what restores the economy to full employment after a macroeconomic shock?

options.label: A
options.text: The government automatically increases spending to close any output gap.

options.label: B
options.text: The central bank lowers interest rates until real GDP reaches potential.

options.label: C
options.text: Flexible wages and prices adjust — wages rise or fall until the SRAS shifts back to intersect AD on the LRAS, restoring full employment.

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregate demand automatically returns to its pre-shock level without any adjustment.

options.label: E
options.text: The LRAS shifts left or right to match wherever the AD-SRAS intersection occurs.

explanation: The CED states explicitly: "In the long run, in the absence of government policy actions, flexible wages and prices will adjust to restore full employment and unemployment will revert to its natural rate." The adjustment mechanism is wages and prices becoming flexible over time - rising when there is an inflationary gap, falling when there is a recessionary gap - which shifts the SRAS until the economy returns to Yf.

options.label: B
options.text: The LRAS shifts left to meet the new lower equilibrium.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Wages rise in response to the lower price level, shifting SRAS left and restoring equilibrium.

options.label: E
options.text: The economy permanently remains in the recessionary gap without government intervention.

explanation: Recessionary gap self-correction: actual GDP < Yf → unemployment > natural rate → excess labor supply → wages gradually fall → production costs fall → SRAS shifts right → new AD-SRAS intersection moves right along the AD curve → real GDP rises back to Yf at a LOWER price level than the original. No policy needed; flexible wages are the mechanism.

options.label: E
